parts.overall: sense 4/5, naturalism 4/5. The prologue is tight, frightening and in good voice, and Tuesday mostly works: the comedy (Nieves, Gail and Derek, Candelaria, Chano, Montesdeoca) is sharp, and the key beats (Vasco's moment in the corridor, Baute's grandmother, Carmen on the steps, the mist) have the right shape and subtext. Most of the problems are continuity slips, not voice: how long Vasco has been on the island, lines for one day that leak knowledge from another (Derek, the arrivals board, the reception door), and a few examine lines reused in places where they no longer describe what is on screen. There are a handful of small voice slips (Chano saying "cariño", a stray "the beach").

sense 4/5, naturalism 4/5. Wednesday is the best-shaped day so far: the Pino, Fermín and Carmen scenes keep the novel's rhythm, every character sounds like their voice-sheet entry, and the running jokes (Fermín dying on the stairs, "Mi mesa", the deported book) land. The real problems are a few logic slips around the scripted moments: at dawn Alan says the truth aloud before he lies, and he drinks the coffee, which spends the game's last gesture on day two. Carmen also demands a cigarette while she is smoking one. Smaller repeats: the van and crate logic doesn't add up, two reveals get no follow-up (Fermín's Artenara, Chano's sponsor theory), and Lolo's Wednesday line gets in ahead of his Friday punchline.

sense 4/5, naturalism 4/5. Thursday is the best-written day so far. Carmen's archive scene is up to the bible's own example, the inquiry reads like a real document, and the comedy (Gail and Derek, Nieves and the suitcase, Derek's fall) lands without stepping on the dread. Most of the problems are continuity: a few lines say things the characters cannot know yet or that contradict the lore (the triangle count, Juan de Quintana's death date, Elena's exact night, Vasco's time home). There are also two places where the line order breaks the logic, and two clues in Baute's office (the framed contract, the 1966 photograph) that Alan passes without a word.

sense 4/5, naturalism 4/5. Friday is the strongest-written day so far. The fight is in Vasco's voice (one-word answers when hurt, then a long, controlled confession), and the Rafa bar is light, warm and well paced; Chano's Telde story and the dusk monologue land without strain. The recurring problems are continuity slips that hurt plot logic: the lab placed "in the museum's basement" when the plot needs it somewhere else, Carmen's "lock" getting no reaction from a man whose family papers say "lock", Carmen's discs-as-mirrors told twice, and Yeray's mumbling being so explicit that Alan's non-reaction ("Sounds rough") reads as a plot convenience, not as a man who is distracted. One line breaks the bracket rule.

sense 3/5, naturalism 4/5. The emotional spine is strong: the waking, the window and the two rules, Rafa's "I know" and the drawing, Inês refusing to absolve him, Pino and Lolo's collar/hair are warm, specific and in voice, and Alan's examine lines get shorter and stranger as rule 7 asks. Most of the problems are continuity left behind by cuts: lines that point at things no longer said (the fax Inês never mentions, "in your time", the radio that is "off"), a count that disagrees with the list on screen, and Nieves saying there are no messages when Inês has been ringing since eight. The other recurring problem is repetition: the "Vasco's up there with Baute, I have to reach him" beat comes three times in the day, and Alan tells Pino about the cistern again after telling her on Thursday.

sense 4/5, naturalism 4/5. Vasco's voice is the chapter's great strength: the lecturer coming alive over the chalk and the light, the dry jokes about Rayco's "original fabric" and the cat flap, the quiet one-word answers to Baute. The refusal and the prayer land with real weight. The problems are mostly about what Vasco knows: three times he talks as if he already knows things he only learns later or never learns (the vault, the word "under", Rayco keeping the sixth disc on him), and twice his lines ignore what he does know (he signed the transfer sheets, so empty sockets can't surprise him; he has been on the dig for weeks without opening Elena's charts). There are smaller slips too: five hundred years against nine hundred, and the discs in straw against discs in cloth.

sense 4/5, naturalism 4/5. Sunday is the best-written day so far. The packing and the queue are spare and inward, Carmen's door, Elena's message and the footwell land hard, and the grille ("He didn't make it.") and "Not now" are earned. The recurring problems are continuity: three lines say the dig radio has been silent "since Friday" or that there has been "not one message", but Alan raised the camp on Saturday and Lolo heard Vasco on the channel that morning. The day also loses track of its own count of the dead and its clock (a five o'clock departure that arrives under stars). Two reveals don't get their obvious follow-up: how Alan knows the cost, and who has the words of the song.

sense 4/5, naturalism 4/5. Monday is the strongest-written day: the finale's mechanics are said aloud by the right people at the right time, Vasco's rim-calls are short and urgent, Carmen's wing mirror and Baute's collapse land, and the confession, the trowel, Nieves and Chano end it in the right register. The problems are small and mostly local: one continuity error with Game I in Alan's speech to Baute, a few lines whose referent is unclear at the moment they're heard ("He's sending the sun back", "So this is how she went", "Tell him. Today."), a time slip or two ("last week", "this morning"), one repeated beat (the Guardia "in an hour" twice), and a confession branch where Vasco says what doesn't hurt but never what does.

parts.part: Across the days: puzzles, the phone box and Ines, background people, close-ups, refusals
parts.overall: sense 4/5, naturalism 4/5. The phone calls are the best writing in this part: Inês is fast, dry and never absolves him, the Pessoa openers land, and Alan's inventory and close-up lines follow rule 7 well (funny early, short and bruised by the weekend: the trowel, the drawing, "I'm putting the nails back"). The background people are funny and stay in one line each. The real problems sit on Saturday. Alan's radio call is set at one o'clock, but Vasco's radio message, which Lolo says he has already heard, cannot go out before the cave's noon at 14:04. Don Lolo, whose voice is "almost nothing" and whose first full sentence is meant to come at the end of the week, gets three long paragraphs here. Beyond that there are small continuity slips (Montesdeoca's age, where Yeray sat, the letter quoted two ways on the same day, the bell "cast in Lisbon and Las Palmas") and a few Inês lines whose logic doesn't hold.
